<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:posetuniv}
  In set theory, the mathematical structure is provided by a set $X$ and a
  binary relation $\leq$ on $X$. Moreover, this relation is required to be
  reflexive, transitive and antisymmetric. Reflexivity,
  $\forall_{x \in X} x \leq x$ is a logical statement that is bivalent.

  In type theory, if we define ${\leq} : {X \to X \to \mathsf{Type}}$, with
  $\mathsf{Type}$ some type universe, then the type encoding reflexivity,
  $\prod_{x : X} x \leq x$, may have more than one element. This is a
  fundamental difference with set theory.

  In Coq, we could instead define ${\leq} : {X \to X \to \texttt{Prop}}$, where
  $\texttt{Prop}$ is Coq's special sort of propositions. This sort is defined
  such that (for instance) reflexivity, \(\forall_{x : X}\,x \leq x\), is again
  in~\(\texttt{Prop}\).

  The crucial difference between these approaches and the univalent approach, is
  that in univalent type theory, we \emph{prove} that something is a proposition
  (truth value). Following Voevodsky, we define a type to be a proposition
  (truth value, subsingleton) if it has at most one element with respect to its
  identity type, i.e.\ up to propositional equality. To define posets, we then
  ask for a witness that the type $x \leq y$ is a proposition for every
  $x,y : X$. This allows us, in the presence of function extensionality (which
  is a consequence of the univalence axiom), to prove that reflexivity and
  transitivity are propositions. For example, for reflexivity, we wish to show
  that the type \(\prod_{x : X} x \leq x\) is a proposition. So let \(f,g\) be
  two elements of this type. By~function extensionality, it suffices to show
  that \(f(x) = g(x)\) for every \(x : X\). But the type of \(f(x)\) and
  \(g(x)\) is \(x \leq x\), which is a proposition by requirement, so \(f(x)\)
  and \(g(x)\) must be (propositionally) equal, as desired. Finally, we require
  $X$ to be a set: any two elements of $X$ are equal in at most one way. This
  ensures, using function extensionality again, that antisymmetry is a
  proposition.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:poset}
  A \emph{poset} $(X,\leq)$ is a set $X$ together with a proposition-valued
  binary relation $\leq : X \to X \to \Omega$ satisfying:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{reflexivity}: $\prod_{x : X} x \leq x$;
  \item \emph{antisymmetry}: $\prod_{x,y : X} x \leq y \to y \leq x \to x = y$;
  \item \emph{transitivity}:
    $\prod_{x,y,z : X} x \leq y \to y \leq z \to x \leq z$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
Notice that we require $\leq$ to take values in $\Omega$, the type of
  propositions in \(\mathcal{U}_0\), cf.\ Example~\ref{ex:posetuniv}. This
  allows us to prove (using function
  extensionality~\cite[Example~3.6.2]{HoTTbook}) that reflexivity and
  transitivity are propositions, i.e.\ there is at most one witness of
  reflexivity and transitivity. We also express this by saying that reflexivity
  and transitivity are properties, rather than structures. Moreover, we restrict
  to $X$ being a set to ensure that antisymmetry is a property, rather than a
  structure.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $X$ and $Y$ be posets. A \emph{poset morphism} from $X$ to $Y$ is a
  function between the underlying sets that preserves the order. We also say
  that the function is \emph{monotone}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:isdirected}
  Let $(X,\leq)$ be a poset and $I$ any type. Given a family $u : I \to X$, we
  often write $u_i$ for $u(i)$. Such a family is called \emph{directed} if \(I\)
  is inhabited (i.e.\ $\squash I$ holds) and
  \(
    \prod_{i,j : I} \squash*{\sum_{k : I}{\pa*{u_i \leq u_k}
        \times \pa*{u_j \leq u_k}}}
  \).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
We use the propositional truncation in the definition above to ensure that
  being directed is a property, rather than a
  structure~(\href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Algebra.DCPO.html\# isaprop_isdirected}{\nolinkurl{isaprop_isdirected}}).

  Firstly, we express that the type $I$ is inhabited by requiring an element of
  $\squash{I}$. This is different from requiring an element of $I$. It is akin
  to the difference (in set theory) between a set $X$ such that
  $\exists {x \in X}$ holds and a pair $(X,x)$ of a set with a chosen element
  $x \in X$.

  Secondly, if we had used an untruncated $\Sigma$ in the second clause of the
  definition, then we would have asked our poset to be equipped with an
  \emph{operation} mapping pairs $(x,y)$ of elements to some \emph{specified}
  element greater than both $x$ and $y$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:directedcomplete}
  An element \(x\) of a poset \(X\) is an \emph{upper bound} of a family
  \(u : I \to X\) if \(u_i \sqsubseteq x\) for every \(i : I\).
   
  It is a \emph{least upper bound} of \(u\) if it is an upper
  bound and \(x \sqsubseteq y\) holds whenever \(y\) is an upper bound of \(u\).

  A poset \(X\) is called \emph{\(\mathcal U\)-directed complete} for a type
  universe \(\mathcal U\) if every directed family in \(X\) indexed by a type in
  \(\mathcal U\) has a least upper bound in \(X\), which we denote by
  \(\bigsqcup_{i : I} u_i\).
  Symbolically,
  \(
    \prod_{I : \mathcal U}\prod_{u : I \to X} \pa*{u\text{ is directed} \to
    \sum_{x : X} x \text{ is a least upper bound of u}}.
  \)

  We call such a poset a \emph{$\mathcal U$-dcpo}.
   
  We shall often simply write dcpo, omitting reference to the type universe.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
Contrary to Definition~\ref{def:isdirected}, directed completeness is not
  phrased with a truncated~\(\Sigma\). This justifies having the least upper
  bound operator \(\bigsqcup\). The reason for this definition of directed
  completeness is that least upper bounds are unique when they
  exist~(\href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Algebra.DCPO.html\# lubsareunique}{\nolinkurl{lubsareunique}}). Moreover, the type expressing
  that an element is a least upper bound for a family can be shown to be a
  proposition using function
  extensionality~(\href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Algebra.DCPO.html\# isaprop_islub}{\nolinkurl{isaprop_islub}}). Hence, for any
  family \(u\), the type of least upper bounds of \(u\) and its propositional
  truncation are equivalent.  This observation also tells us, using function
  extensionality again, that the type expressing that a poset is directed
  complete is also a
  proposition~(\href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Algebra.DCPO.html\# isaprop_isdirectedcomplete}{\nolinkurl{isaprop_isdirectedcomplete}}), i.e.\ it
  is a property of the poset.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
In classical mathematics, a dcpo is usually defined as a poset such that every
  directed \emph{subset} has a least upper bound. We have formulated our version
  using \emph{families}, because in our type-theoretic framework functions are
  primitive, unlike in set theory where sets are primitive and functions are
  encoded as particular sets. Another reason for preferring families is that we
  work in the absence of propositional resizing, so that we must pay attention
  to size and therefore only ask for least upper bounds of \emph{small} directed
  subsets. This point is explained and worked out in detail in
  \cite[Section~5]{deJongEscardo2021b} to which we refer the interested
  reader. Here we limit ourselves to saying that working with families is more
  direct, and that for the Scott model we will only need to consider simple
  \(\mathsf{N}\)-indexed directed families anyway.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $D$ and $E$ be dcpos. A poset morphism from $D$ to $E$ is a \emph{dcpo
    morphism} (or \emph{continuous}) if it preserves least upper bounds of
  directed families. That is, if \(u : I \to D\) is a directed family, then
  \(f\pa*{\bigsqcup_{i : I}u_i}\) is the least upper bound of
  \(f \circ u : I \to E\).
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{monotoneforfree}
  Let $D$ and $E$ be dcpos. If $f$ is a function \textup{(}on the underlying
  types\textup{)} from $D$ to $E$ preserving least upper bounds of directed
  families, then $f$ is order preserving.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $f : D \to E$ be a morphism of dcpos and suppose $x,y : D$ with
  $x \leq y$. Consider the family $\mathsf{1} + \mathsf{1} \to D$ defined as
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(\star) \mapsto x$ and $\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star) \mapsto y$. This family is easily
  seen to be directed and its least upper bound is $y$. Now $f$ preserves this
  least upper bound, so $f(x) \leq f(y)$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
Every morphism of dcpos preserves directed families. That is, if $f : D \to E$
  is a morphism of dcpos and $u$ is a directed family in $D$, then $f \circ u$
  is a directed family in $E$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Using monotonicity of \(f\).
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- therm-1: body_md -->
\label{dcpoofdcpomor}
  Let $D$ and $E$ be dcpos. The morphisms from $D$ to $E$ form a dcpo with the
  pointwise order.
<!-- end therm-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The least upper bound of a directed family of dcpo morphisms is also given
  pointwise. The proof only differs from the standard proof of
  \cite[Theorem~4.2]{Streicher2006} in that it uses directed families, rather
  than subsets. One may consult the formalisation for the technical details.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:dcpowithbottom}
  A \emph{dcpo with $\bot$} is a dcpo $D$ together with a least element in $D$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- therm-2: body_md -->
\label{dcpowithbot_ofdcpomor}
  Let $D$ be a dcpo and let $E$ be a dcpo with $\bot$. Ordered pointwise, the
  morphisms from $D$ to $E$ form a dcpo with $\bot$, which we denote by $E^D$.
<!-- end therm-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Since the order is pointwise, the least morphism from $D$ to $E$ is simply
  given by mapping every element in $D$ to the least element in $E$. The rest is
  as in Theorem~\ref{dcpoofdcpomor}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- therm-3: body_md -->
\label{leastfixedpoint}
  Let $D$ be a dcpo with $\bot$. There is a continuous function
  $\mu : D^D \to D$ that sends each continuous function to its least fixed
  point. In fact, $\mu$ satisfies:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $f(\mu(f)) = \mu(f)$ for every continuous $f : D \to D$;
  \item for every continuous $f : D \to D$ and each $d : D$, if $f(d) \leq d$,
    then $\mu(f) \leq d$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end therm-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
We have formalised the proof of \cite[Theorem 2.1.19]{AbramskyJung1994}. We
  sketch the main construction here. For each natural number $n$, define
  $\mathsf{iter}(n) : D^D \to D$ as
  \[
    \mathsf{iter}(n)(f) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv f^n(\bot) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    \underbrace{f(f(\dots(f}_{n\text{ times}}(\bot))\dots)).
  \]
  By induction on $n$, one may show that every $\mathsf{iter}(n)$ is
  continuous. Then, the assignment $n~\mapsto~{\mathsf{iter}(n)}$ is a directed
  family in $D^{\pa*{D^D}}$. Finally, one defines $\mu$ as the least upper bound
  of this directed family. Recall that least upper bounds in the exponential are
  given pointwise, so that $\mu(f) = \bigsqcup_{n : \mathsf{N}} f^n(\bot)$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
Directed completeness of $\mathsf{N}_{\bot}$ implies \textup{LPO}.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathsf{N}_{\bot}$ is ($\mathcal{U}_0$-)directed complete. Let
  $\alpha : \mathsf{N} \to \mathsf{2}$ be an arbitrary binary sequence. Define the family
  $\beta : \mathsf{N} \to \mathsf{N}_{\bot}$ as
  \[
    \beta(n) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    \begin{cases}
      \operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k) &\text{if $k$ is the least integer $\leq n$ such that $\alpha(k) =
        1$;} \\
      \operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star) &\text{else}.
    \end{cases}
  \]
  Then $\beta$ is directed, so by assumption, it has a supremum $s$ in
  $\mathsf{N}_{\bot}$. By the induction principle of sum-types, we can decide whether
  $s = \operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k)$ for some $k : \mathsf{N}$ or $s = \operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star)$. The former implies
  $\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} \alpha(k) = 1$ and we claim that the latter implies
  $\prod_{n : \mathsf{N}} \alpha(n) = 0$. For suppose that \(s = \operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star)\) and
  let \(n : \mathsf{N}\). Since \(\mathsf{2}\) has decidable equality, it suffices to show
  that \(\alpha(n) \neq 1\). Assume for a contradiction that \(\alpha(n) =
  1\). Then \(\beta(n) = \operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k)\) for some natural number \(k \leq n\). Using
  that \(s\) is the supremum of \(\beta\) yields:
  \(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k) = \beta(n) \leq_\bot s = \operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star)\). By definition of the order
  we also have the reverse inequality \(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star) \leq_\bot \operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k)\). Hence,
  \(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star) = \operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(k)\) by antisymmetry, which is a contradiction, so
  \(\alpha(n) \neq 1\) as desired.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
Let $X$ be any type. Define the \emph{lifting of X} as
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \sum_{P : \Omega} (P \to X).
  \]
  Strictly speaking, we should have written $\operatorname{\mathsf{pr_1}}(P) \to X$, because
  elements of $\Omega$ are pairs of types and witnesses that these types are
  subsingletons. We will almost always suppress reference to these witnesses in
  this paper.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{lift_least}
  For any type $X$, the type $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ has a distinguished element
  \[
    \bot_X \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \pa*{\mathsf{0},\textup{\textsf{from-}}\mathsf{0}_X} :
    \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X),
  \]
  where $\textup{\textsf{from-}}\mathsf{0}_X$ is the unique function from $\mathsf{0}$
  to $X$.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{lift_embedding}
  There is a canonical map $ \eta_X \colon X \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X) $ defined by
  \[
    \eta_X(x) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv (\mathsf{1},\lambda t.x).
  \]
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
We take
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} : \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X) \to \Omega$ to be the first projection. The function
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{value}} : \prod_{l : \operatorname{\mathcal L} (X)} \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (l) \to X$ is given by:
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (P,\varphi) (p) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \varphi (p)$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lifteqchar}
  Let $X$ be any type and let $l, m : \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$. The following are logically
  equivalent\footnote{In fact, there is a type equivalence. One can prove this
    using univalence and a generalised structure identity principle, cf.\
    \cite[\texttt{LiftingIdentityViaSIP}]{TypeTopology}.}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $l = m$\textup{;}
  \item\label{lifteqchar-2}
    $\sum_{e : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)} \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l) \circ
    \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e) \sim \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
First of all, the characterisation of the identity type of
  \(\Sigma\)-types~\cite[Theorem~2.7.2]{HoTTbook} yields:
  \begin{equation*}\label{id-type-of-sum-type}
    \tag{\(\dagger\)}
    \pa*{l = m} \simeq \sum_{e' : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) = \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)}
    \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e',\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l))=\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m).
  \end{equation*}
  Thus we only have to show that the right-hand side of
  \eqref{id-type-of-sum-type} is logically equivalent to \eqref{lifteqchar-2} in the lemma.
  Suppose first that we have \(e' : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) = \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)\) and an
  equality \break \({p : \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e',\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l)) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)}\). Then
  \[
    e \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{eqtoiff}(e') : {\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) \leftrightarrow
      \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)}.
  \]
  Using path induction on \(e'\), we can prove that
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l) \circ \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e) =
  \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e',\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l))$. Together with $p$, this equality
  implies
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l) \circ \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e) \sim \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)$,
  as desired.

  Conversely, suppose $e : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (l) \leftrightarrow \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (m)$ and
  $v : \operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (l) \circ \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e) \sim \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)$. By
  propositional extensionality, we obtain $e' : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) = \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)$
  from $e$. From $e'$ we can get an equivalence
  $\mathsf{idtoeqv}(e') : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (l) \simeq \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)$.  Furthermore,
  using path induction on $e'$, one can prove that
  \begin{equation*}\label{transporteq}
    \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e',\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l)) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l) \circ
    (\mathsf{idtoeqv}(e'))^{-1}.\tag{$\ast$}
  \end{equation*}
  Hence, it suffices to show that the right-hand side of~\eqref{transporteq} is
  equal to \(\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)\). The homotopy \(v\) yields
  \(\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l) \circ \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)\) by function
  extensionality, so it suffices to prove that
  \((\mathsf{idtoeqv}(e'))^{-1} = \operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(e)\). But these are both
  functions with codomain \(\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l)\), which is a proposition, so they are
  equal by function extensionality.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
Given $f : X \to \operatorname{\mathcal L} (Y)$, the \emph{Kleisli extension}
  $f^\# : \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X) \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Y)$ is defined by:
  \[
    f^\#(P,\varphi) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \Bigg(\sum_{p : P} \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (f(\varphi(p))),
    \psi\Bigg),
  \]
  where $\psi(p,d) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (f(\varphi(p)))(d)$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- therm-4: body_md -->
\label{lifting-is-monad}
  The above constructions yield a monad structure on $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$, i.e.\ the
  Kleisli laws hold \textup{(}pointwise\textup{)}:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\pa*{\eta_X}^\# \sim \operatorname{id}_{\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)}$;
  \item $f^\# \circ \eta_X \sim f$ for any $f : X \to \operatorname{\mathcal L} (Y)$;
  \item\label{lifting-is-monad-3}
    $g^\# \circ f^\# \sim (g^\# \circ f)^\#$ for any $f : X \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Y)$
    and $g : Y \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Z)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end therm-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The proofs are straightforward thanks to Lemma~\ref{lifteqchar}.
  Item~\eqref{lifting-is-monad-3} is essentially the
  associativity of $\Sigma$, i.e.\ equivalence between
  $\sum_{a : A} \sum_{b : B(a)} C(a,b)$ and
  $\sum_{(a,b) : \sum_{a : A} B(a)} C(a,b)$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- therm-5: body_md -->
\label{liftofsetisaset}
  If $X$ is a set, then so is its lifting $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$.
<!-- end therm-5 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lifteqchar}, we have:
  \[
    l = m \simeq \sum_{e : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) = \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)}
    \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e,\operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (l)) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (m).
  \]
  Since $X$ is a set, the type
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}(e,\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(l)) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(m)$ is a proposition. So, if
  we can prove that $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) = \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(m)$ is a proposition, then the
  right hand side is a proposition indexed sum of propositions, which is again a
  proposition.

  So let us prove that if $P$ and $Q$ are propositions, then so is $P = Q$. At
  first glance, it might seem like one needs univalence (for propositions) to
  prove this, but in fact propositional extensionality suffices. By
  \cite[Lemma~3.11]{Krausetal2017} (applied to the type of propositions), it
  suffices to give for every proposition \(R\), a (weakly) constant (i.e.\ any
  two of its values are equal) endomap on $P = R$. But the composition
  \[
    (P = R) \to (P \leftrightarrow R) \xrightarrow{\text{PropExt}} (P = R)
  \]
  is weakly constant, because $P \leftrightarrow R$ is a proposition, so this
  finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- therm-6: body_md -->
\label{liftofsetisdcpo}
  If $X$ is a set, then $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ is a dcpo with $\bot$ with the following
  order:
  \[
    l \sqsubseteq m \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) \to l = m.
  \]
<!-- end therm-6 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
First of
  all, we should prove that $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ is a poset with the specified order. In
  particular, $\sqsubseteq$ should be proposition-valued. If $X$ is a set, then
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(l) \to l = m$ is a function type into a proposition and therefore
  a proposition itself.

  Reflexivity and transitivity of $\sqsubseteq$ are easily verified. Moreover,
  $\sqsubseteq$ is seen to be antisymmetric using Lemma~\ref{lifteqchar}.

  The $\bot$ element of $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ is given by $\bot_X$ from
  Definition~\ref{lift_least}.

  The construction of the least upper bound of a directed family is the most
  challenging part of the proof. Let \(u : I \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)\) be a directed family
  in \(\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)\). Consider the diagram (of solid arrows):

  \begin{center}
    \begin{tikzcd}
      \sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)
      \ar[rr,"\varphi : {(i,d)} \mapsto \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(u_i)(d)"]
      \ar[dr,"\tosquash{-}"']
      & & X \\
      & \squash*{\sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)}
      \ar[ur, dashed, "\psi"']
    \end{tikzcd}
  \end{center}
  We are going to construct the dashed map \(\psi\) that makes the diagram
  commute and define the least upper bound of \(u\) as:
  \(\pa*{\squash*{\sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)},\psi}\). Truncating the type is
  necessary, as \(\sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)\) may have more than one element
  if \(I\) is not a proposition. The difficulty lies in the fact that the
  universal property of the truncation only tells us how to define maps into
  \emph{propositions}. But \(X\) is a \emph{set}. We solve this problem using
  \cite[Theorem~5.4]{Krausetal2017}, which says that every weakly constant
  function \(f : A \to B\) to a set \(B\) factors through \(\squash*{A}\). That
  \(f\) is weakly constant means that \(f(a) = f(a')\) for every \(a,a' :
  A\). So, to construct \(\psi\), we only need to prove that the top map
  \(\varphi\) in the diagram is weakly constant. Let \((i,d_i) , (j,d_j)\) be two
  elements of the domain of \(\varphi\). We are to prove that
  \(\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(u_i)(d_i) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(u_j)(d_j)\). As \(X\) is a set, this is a
  proposition. Therefore, using that \(u\) is directed, we obtain \(k : I\) with
  \(u_i,u_j \sqsubseteq u_k\). But \(d_i : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)\) and
  \(d_j : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_j)\), so \(u_i = u_k = u_j\) by definition of the
  order. Hence,
  \(\varphi(i,d_i) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(u_i)(d_i) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(u_j)(d_j) = \varphi(j,d_j)\),
  as we wished to show.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- therm-7: body_md -->
\label{Kleisliextensioncont}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be sets and $f : X \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Y)$ any function. The Kleisli
  extension $f^\# : \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X) \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Y)$ is a morphism of dcpos.
<!-- end therm-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $v$ be the least upper bound of a directed family $u : I \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ in
  $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$. Proving that $f^\#$ is monotone is quite easy. By monotonicity,
  $f^\#(v)$ is an upper bound for the family $f^\# \circ u$. We are left to
  prove that it is the least. Suppose that $l : \operatorname{\mathcal L}(Y)$ is another upper bound
  for the family $f^\#\circ u$, i.e.\ $l \sqsupseteq f^\#(u_i)$ for every
  $i : I$. We must show that $f^\#(v) \sqsubseteq l$. To this end, assume we
  have $q : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(f^\#(v))$. We must prove that $f^\#(v) = l$.

  From $q$, we obtain $p : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(v)$ by definition of $f^\#$. By our
  construction of suprema in $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(X)$ and the fact that $f^\#(v) = l$ is a
  proposition, we may in fact assume that we have an element $i : I$ and
  $d_i : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(u_i)$. But $l \sqsupseteq f^\#(u_i)$, so using $d_i$, we get
  the equality $l = f^\#(u_i)$. Since $v$ is an upper bound for $u$, the term
  $d_i$ also yields $u_i = v$. In particular, $l = f^\#(u_i) = f^\#(v)$, as
  desired.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{liftfunctoreq}
  Finally, one could define the functor $\operatorname{\mathcal L}$ from the Kleisli extension and
  unit by putting $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(f) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv (\eta_Y \circ f)^\#$ for any
  $f : X \to Y$. However, it is equivalent and easier to directly define
  $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(f)$ by postcomposition:
  $\operatorname{\mathcal L}(f)(P,\varphi) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv (P,f \circ \varphi)$.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{liftasfree}
  We remark that lifting may be regarded as a free construction, in more than
  one way in fact. This result should be compared to
  \cite[Theorem~5]{AltenkirchDanielssonKraus2017}, where Altenkirch et al.\
  exhibit their QIIT as the free $\omega$-cpo with a least element (cf.\
  Section~\ref{sec:relatedwork}).

  By~\cite[Theorems 21 and 23]{deJongEscardo2021a}, the lifting of a set \(X\)
  can be regarded both as the free pointed dcpo on \(X\) and as the free
  subsingleton complete poset on \(X\). In our predicative setting, some care
  should be taken in formulating these statements. We do not go into the details
  here and instead refer the interested reader to~\cite{deJongEscardo2021a}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
The \emph{PCF types} are inductively defined as:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\iota$ is a type, the \emph{base type};
  \item for every two types $\sigma$ and $\tau$, there is a \emph{function type}
    $\sigma \Rightarrow \tau$.
  \end{enumerate}
  As usual, $\Rightarrow$ will be right associative, so we write
  $\sigma \Rightarrow \tau \Rightarrow \rho$ for
  $\sigma \Rightarrow (\tau \Rightarrow \rho)$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{def:PCFterms}
  The \emph{PCF terms of PCF type $\sigma$} are inductively generated by:
  \begin{center}
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\mathsf{zero}} \text{ of type } \iota$}
    \DisplayProof \quad
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}} \text{ of type } \iota \Rightarrow \iota$}
    \DisplayProof\vspace{0.5cm}\\
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} \text{ of type } \iota \Rightarrow \iota$}
    \DisplayProof \quad
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}}} \text{ of type } {\iota \Rightarrow \iota \Rightarrow \iota
        \Rightarrow \iota}$}
    \DisplayProof \vspace{0.5cm}\\
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}_{\sigma,\tau}} \text{ of type } \sigma \Rightarrow \tau \Rightarrow
      \sigma$}
    \DisplayProof \quad \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}_{\sigma,\tau,\rho}} \text{ of type } (\sigma \Rightarrow \tau
      \Rightarrow \rho) \Rightarrow \break (\sigma \Rightarrow \tau) \Rightarrow
      \sigma \Rightarrow \rho$}
    \DisplayProof\vspace{0.5cm}\\
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$t : \iota$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}_\sigma} \text{ of type } (\sigma \Rightarrow \sigma)
      \Rightarrow \sigma$}
    \DisplayProof \quad
    \AxiomC{$s \text{ of type } \sigma \Rightarrow \tau$}
    \AxiomC{$t \text{ of type } \tau$}
    \BinaryInfC{$(st) \text{ of type } \tau$}
    \DisplayProof
  \end{center}
  We will often drop the parentheses in the final clause, as well as the PCF
  type subscripts in \({\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}_{\sigma,\tau}}\), \({\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}_{\sigma,\tau,\rho}}\)
  and \({\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}_\sigma}\). Finally, we employ the convention that the parentheses
  associate to the left, i.e.\ we write $rst$~for~$(rs)t$.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{def:PCFnumerals}
  For any $n : \mathsf{N}$, let us write $\underline n$ for the $n$th PCF numeral,
  defined inductively as:
  \[
    \underline 0 \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv {\mathsf{zero}};\quad \underline {n+1} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    \operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}\,\underline n.
  \]
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{def:small-step}
  Define the \emph{small-step pre-relation} $\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}}$ of type
  \[
    \prod_{\sigma : \text{PCF types}} \text{PCF terms of type $\sigma$} \to
    \text{PCF terms of type $\sigma$} \to \mathcal{U}_0
  \]
  as the inductive family generated by:
  \begin{center}
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}\underline 0\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}}\underline 0$}
    \DisplayProof \quad \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}\underline {n+1}\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}}\underline n$}
    \DisplayProof \quad \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,\underline 0\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} s$} \DisplayProof
    \quad \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,\underline {n+1}\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$}
    \DisplayProof \vspace{0.5cm}
    \\
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}} st\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} s$} \DisplayProof \quad
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$f \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{${\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}}fgt\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} ft(gt)$} \DisplayProof \quad
    \AxiomC{\phantom{$f\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$}}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} f\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} f(\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} f)$} \DisplayProof
    \quad \AxiomC{$f\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} g$} \UnaryInfC{$ft\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} gt$}
    \DisplayProof \vspace{0.5cm}
    \\
    \AxiomC{$s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} \operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} t$} \DisplayProof
    \quad \AxiomC{$s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} \operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} t$} \DisplayProof
    \quad \AxiomC{$r \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} r'$}
    \UnaryInfC{$\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,r \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} \operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,r'$}
    \DisplayProof
  \end{center}

  We have been unable to prove that $s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$ is a proposition for
  every suitable PCF terms $s$~and~$t$. The difficulty is that one cannot
  perform induction on \emph{both} \(s\) and \(t\). However, conceptually,
  $s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$ should be a proposition, as (by inspection of the
  definition), there is at most one way by which we obtained
  $s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t$. Moreover, for technical reasons that will become apparent
  later, we really want $\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}}$ to be propostion-valued.

  We solve the problem by defining the \emph{small-step relation} $\mathbin{\triangleright}$ as
  the propositional truncation of~$\mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}}$, i.e.\
  $s \mathbin{\triangleright} t \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \squash{s \mathbin{\widetilde{\triangleright}} t}$.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
Benedikt Ahrens pointed out that in an impredicative framework, one could use
  propositional resizing and an impredicative encoding, i.e.\ by defining
  $\mathbin{\triangleright}$ as a $\Pi$-type of all suitable proposition-valued
  relations. This is similar to the situation in set theory, where one would
  define $\mathbin{\triangleright}$ as an intersection. Specifically, say that a relation
  \[
    R : \prod_{\sigma : \text{PCF types}} \pa*{\text{PCF terms of type
        \(\sigma\)} \to \text{PCF terms of type \(\sigma\)} \to \Omega_{\mathcal
        U_0}}
  \] is \emph{suitable} if it closed under all the clauses of
  Definition~\ref{def:small-step}, i.e.\
  \(R\pa*{\iota,\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} \underline 0,\underline 0}\),
  \(R\pa*{\iota,\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} \underline{n+1},\underline n}\), etc.\ are all
  inhabited.  We could define
  \(s \mathbin{\triangleright}_{\text{impred}} t \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \prod_{R \text{ suitable}}
  R(\sigma,s,t)\). But notice the increase in universe level:
  \[
    \mathbin{\triangleright}_{\text{impred}} : \prod_{\sigma : \text{PCF types}}
    \pa*{\text{PCF terms of type \(\sigma\)} \to \text{PCF terms of type
        \(\sigma\)} \to \Omega_{\mathcal U_1}}.
  \]
  So because of this increase, \(\mathbin{\triangleright}_{\text{impred}}\) itself is not one
  of the suitable relations. Therefore \(\mathbin{\triangleright}_{\text{impred}}\) does not
  satisfy the appropriate universal property in being the least relation closed
  under the clauses in Definition~\ref{def:small-step}. With propositional
  resizing we could resize \(\mathbin{\triangleright}_{\text{impred}}\) to a
  \(\mathcal U_0\)-valued relation satisfying the appropriate universal
  property.
   
  The advantage of using the propositional truncation above is that it does
  satisfy the right universal property even without propositional resizing.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{def:refltransclos}
  Let $R : X \to X \to \Omega$ be a relation on a type $X$. We define the
  \emph{reflexive transitive closure} $R^\ast$ of $R$ by
  $x R^\ast y \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \squash*{x R_\ast y}$, where $R_\ast$ is as above.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{refltransreduce}
  Let $r', r, s$ and $t$ be PCF terms of type $\iota$. If
  $r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast r$, then
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{refltransreduce-1} $\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r$;
  \item $\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \operatorname{\mathsf{pred}} r$;
  \item $\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,r$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Moreover, if $f$ and $g$ are PCF terms of type $\sigma\Rightarrow\tau$ and
  $f \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast g$, then $f t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast g t$ for any PCF term $t$ of
  type $\sigma$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We only
  prove~\eqref{refltransreduce-1} the rest is similar. Suppose
  $r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast r'$.  Since $\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r' \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r$ is a
  proposition, we may assume that we actually have a term $p$ of type
  $r' \mathbin{\triangleright}_\ast r'$. Now we can perform induction on $p$. The cases were
  $p$ is formed using $\mathsf{refl}$ or $\mathsf{trans}$ are easy. If $p$ is
  formed by $\mathsf{extend}$, then we get a term of type
  $r \mathbin{\triangleright} r' \equiv \squash{r \widetilde{\mathbin{\triangleright}} r'}$. Again, as we
  are proving a proposition, we may suppose the existence of a term of type
  $r \widetilde{\mathbin{\triangleright}} r'$. By Definition~\ref{def:small-step}, we
  then get $\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r'\widetilde{\mathbin{\triangleright}}\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r$. This in turn yields,
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r'\mathbin{\triangleright}\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r$ and finally we use $\mathsf{extend}$ to get the
  desired $\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r'\mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}} r$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
Inductively assign to each PCF type $\sigma$ a dcpo with $\bot$ as follows:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\densem{\iota} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \operatorname{\mathcal L}(\mathsf{N})$;
  \item
    $\densem{\sigma \Rightarrow \tau} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    \densem{\tau}^{\densem{\sigma}}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Recall that if $D$ and $E$ are dcpos with $\bot$, then $E^D$ is the dcpo with
  $\bot$ of dcpo morphisms from $D$ to $E$, with pointwise ordering and
  pointwise least upper bounds.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
Define for each PCF term $t$ of PCF type $\sigma$ a term $\densem{t}$ of type
  $\densem{\sigma}$, by the following inductive clauses:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\densem{\mathsf{zero}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \eta(0)$;
  \item $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \operatorname{\mathcal L}(s)$, where
    $s : \mathsf{N} \to \mathsf{N}$ is the successor function;
  \item $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \operatorname{\mathcal L}(p)$, where
    $p : \mathsf{N} \to \mathsf{N}$ is the predecessor function;
  \item
    $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}}} :
    \densem{\iota\Rightarrow\iota\Rightarrow\iota\Rightarrow\iota}$ is defined
    using the Kleisli extension as: $\lambda x,y.\pa*{\chi_{x,y}}^{\#}$, where
    \[
      \chi_{x,y}(n) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
      \begin{cases}
        x &\text{if } n = 0; \\
        y &\text{else};
      \end{cases}
    \]
  \item $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \lambda x, y . x$;
  \item $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \lambda f, g, x . (f (x)) (g (x))$;
  \item $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}} \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mu$, where $\mu$ is the least fixed
    point operator from Theorem~\ref{leastfixedpoint}.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
Of course, there are some things to be proved here. Namely,
  $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}}, \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}}, \dots, \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}}$ all need to be dcpo
  morphisms. In the case of $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}}$ and $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}}$, we simply
  appeal to Theorem~\ref{Kleisliextensioncont} and
  Remark~\ref{liftfunctoreq}. For $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}}$, this is
  Theorem~\ref{leastfixedpoint}. The continuity of
  $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}}, \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}}$ and $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}}}$ can be verified directly,
  as done in the formalisation (\href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Partiality.PCF.html\# k_dcpo}{\nolinkurl{k_dcpo}},
  \href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Partiality.PCF.html\# s_dcpo}{\nolinkurl{s_dcpo}},
  \href{https://tomdjong.github.io/Scott-PCF-UniMath/UniMath. Partiality.PCF.html\# lifted_ifz}{\nolinkurl{lifted_ifz}}). It is however, unenlightning and
  tedious, so we omit the details here.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{densemnumeral}
  For every natural number $n$, we have $\densem{\underline n} = \eta (n)$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $n$. The $n\equiv 0$ case is by definition of
  $\densem{\underline 0}$. Suppose $\densem{\underline m} = \eta (m)$ for a
  natural number $m$. Then,
  \begin{alignat*}{2}
    \densem{\underline {m+1}} &= \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}}(\densem{\underline
                                m}) \\
                              &= \operatorname{\mathcal L}(s)(\eta (m))\quad&&\text{(by induction
                                                          hypothesis)} \\
                              &= \eta(m + 1) \quad&&\text{(by definition of
                                                    the lift functor)},
  \end{alignat*}
  as desired.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- therm-8: body_md -->
Let $s$ and $t$ be any PCF terms of PCF type $\sigma$. If
  $s \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast t$, then $\densem{s} = \densem{t}$.
<!-- end therm-8 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Since the carriers of dcpos are defined to be sets, the type
  \(\densem{s} = \densem{t}\) is a proposition. Therefore, we can use induction
  on the derivation of \(s \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast t\). We use the Kleisli monad laws in
  proving some of the cases. For example, one step is to prove that
  \[
    \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,\underline{n+1}} = \densem{t}.
  \]
  This may be proved by the following chain of equalities:
  \begin{alignat*}{2}
    \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t\,\underline{n+1}} &=
    \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t}(\densem{\underline{n+1}}) \\
    &= \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}} s\,t}(\eta(n+1))\quad&&\text{(by
      Proposition~\ref{densemnumeral})} \\
    &= (\chi_{\densem{s},\densem{t}})^\#(\eta(n+1)) \quad&&\text{(by definition
      of $\densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}}}$)} \\
    &= \chi_{\densem{s},\densem{t}}(n+1) \quad&&\text{(by
      Theorem~\ref{lifting-is-monad})} \\ &= \densem{t}.\tag*{\qedhere}
  \end{alignat*}
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- therm-9: body_md -->
\label{Adequacy}
  Let $t$ be a PCF term of PCF type $\iota$. Then,
  \[
    \prod_{p : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (\densem{t})} t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \underline{\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}
      (\densem{t}) (p)}.
  \]
  Equivalently, for every $n : \mathsf{N}$, it holds that
  $ \densem{t} = \densem{\underline{n}} $ implies
  $t \mathbin{\triangleright^{\ast}} {\underline n}$.
<!-- end therm-9 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
For every PCF type $\sigma$, define a relation
  \[
    R_\sigma : \textup{PCF terms of type $\sigma$} \to \densem{\sigma} \to \Omega
  \]
  by induction on $\sigma$:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item
    $t R_\iota d \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \prod_{p : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}} (d)} t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast
    \underline {\operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(d)(p)}$;
  \item
    $s R_{\tau \Rightarrow \rho} f \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \prod_{t : \text{PCF terms of
        type $\tau$}} \prod_{d : \densem{\tau}} \pa*{t R_\tau d \to st R_\rho
      f(d)}$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We sometimes omit the type subscript $\sigma$ in $R_\sigma$.
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{logicalrelationsmall-step}
  Let $s$ and $t$ be PCF terms of type $\sigma$ and let $d$ be an element
  of~$\densem{\sigma}$. If $s \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast t$ and $t R_\sigma d$, then
  $s R_\sigma d$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By induction on $\sigma$, making use of the last part of
  Lemma~\ref{refltransreduce}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{logicalrelationconstants}
  For $t$ equal to
  $\mathsf{zero}, {\operatorname{\mathsf{succ}}}, {\operatorname{\mathsf{pred}}}, {\operatorname{\mathsf{ifz}}}, {\operatorname{\mathsf{k}}}$ or
  ${\operatorname{\mathsf{s}}}$, we have: $t R \densem{t}$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By the previous lemma and Lemma~\ref{refltransreduce}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{logicalrelationbottom}
  Let $\sigma$ be a PCF type and let $\bot$ be the least element of
  $\densem{\sigma}$. Then, $t R_\sigma \bot$ for any PCF term $t$ of type
  $\sigma$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
By induction on $\sigma$. For the base type, this holds vacuously. For
  function types, it follows by induction hypothesis and the pointwise ordering.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
The logical relation is closed under directed suprema. That is, for every PCF
  term $t$ of type $\sigma$ and every directed family
  $d : I \to \densem{\sigma}$, if $t R_\sigma d_i$ for every $i : I$, then
  $t R_\sigma \bigsqcup_{i : I}d_i$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
This proof is somewhat different from the classical proof, so we spell out the
  details. We prove the lemma by induction on $\sigma$.

  The case when $\sigma$ is a function type is easy, because least upper bounds
  are calculated pointwise and so it reduces to an application of the induction
  hypothesis. We concentrate on the case when $\sigma \equiv \iota$ instead.

  Recall that $\bigsqcup_{i : I} d_i$ is given by
  $\pa*{\squash*{\sum_{i : I} \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(d_i)}, \varphi}$, where $\varphi$ is the
  factorisation of
  \[
    \sum_{i : I} \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(d_i) \to \operatorname{\mathcal L}(\mathsf{N}), \quad (i, p_i) \mapsto
    \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(d_i)(p_i)
  \]
  through $\squash*{\sum_{i : I} \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(d_i)}$.

  We are tasked with proving that $t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \underline{\varphi (p)}$ for
  every $p : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}\pa*{\bigsqcup_{i : I}d_i}$. So assume that
  $p : \squash*{\sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(d_i)}$. Since we are trying to prove a
  proposition (as $\mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast$ is proposition-valued), we may actually
  assume that we have $(j,p_{j}) : \sum_{i : I}\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(d_i)$.  By definition
  of $\varphi$ we have: $\varphi (p) = \operatorname{\mathsf{value}}(d_{j})(p_{j})$ and by assumption we
  know that $t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \underline{\operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (d_{j}) (p_{j})}$, so we
  are done.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
For every PCF type $\sigma$, we have
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}_\sigma R_{(\sigma \Rightarrow \sigma)\Rightarrow \sigma}
  \densem{\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}}_\sigma}$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $\sigma\Rightarrow\sigma$ and let
  $f : \densem{\sigma\Rightarrow\sigma}$ such that
  $t R_{\sigma\Rightarrow\sigma} f$. We are to prove that
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} t R_\sigma \mu(f)$.

  By definition of $\mu$ and the previous lemma, it suffices to prove that
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} t R_\sigma f^n(\bot)$ where $\bot$ is the least element of
  $\densem{\sigma}$ for every natural number $n$. We do so by induction on $n$.

  The base case is an application of Lemma~\ref{logicalrelationbottom}.

  Now suppose that $\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} t R_\sigma f^m(\bot)$. Then, using
  $t R_{\sigma\Rightarrow\sigma} f$, we find:
  $t(\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} t) R_\sigma f(f^m(\bot))$. Hence, by
  Lemma~\ref{logicalrelationsmall-step}, we obtain the desired
  $\operatorname{\mathsf{fix}} t R_\sigma f^{m+1}(\bot)$, completing our proof by induction.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{mainlemma}
  For every PCF term $t$ of type $\sigma$, we have $t R_\sigma \densem{t}$.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
The proof is by induction on $t$. The base cases are taken care of by
  Lemma~\ref{logicalrelationconstants} and the previous lemma. For the inductive
  step, suppose $t$ is a PCF term of type $\sigma\Rightarrow\tau$. By induction
  hypothesis, $ts R_\tau \densem{ts}$ for every PCF term $s$ of type $\sigma$,
  but $\densem{ts} \equiv \densem{t}\densem{s}$, so we are done.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Take $\sigma$ to be the base type $\iota$ in Lemma~\ref{mainlemma}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{def:semidecidable}
  A proposition \(Q\) is \emph{semidecidable} if it is equivalent to
  \(\exists_{n_1 : \mathsf{N}}\cdots\exists_{n_k : \mathsf{N}}P(n_1,\dots,n_k)\) where
  \(k\) is some natural number and \(P : \mathsf{N}^k \to \Omega\) is a
  proposition-valued family such that \(P(m_1,\dots,m_k)\) is decidable for every
  \((m_1,\dots,m_k) : \mathsf{N}^k\).
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{soundnesscompadequacyprop}
  Let $t$ be a PCF term of type $\iota$. We have the following logical
  equivalences
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\densem{t}) \enspace\longleftrightarrow\enspace \sum_{n : \mathsf{N}}
    t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast {\underline{n}} \enspace\longleftrightarrow\enspace
    \squash*{\sum_{n : \mathsf{N}} t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \underline {n}}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
We start by proving the first logical equivalence. The second then follows
  from the fact that $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\densem{t})$ is a proposition. Suppose $p$ is
  of type $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\densem{t})$. By computational adequacy, we find that
  $t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast {\underline {\operatorname{\mathsf{value}} (\densem{t}) (p)}}$, so we are
  done.

  Conversely, suppose that we are given a natural number $n$ such that
  $t \mathbin{\triangleright}^\ast \underline n$. Soundness and
  Proposition~\ref{densemnumeral} then yield $\densem{t} = \eta(n)$. Now
  $\star : \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\eta(n))$, so we may transport along the equality to get
  an element of $\operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\densem{t})$.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
For every PCF term $t$ of type $\iota$, we have:
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}\pa*{\densem{t}} \longleftrightarrow \exists_{n : \mathsf{N}}\exists_{k
      : \mathsf{N}} t \mathbin{\triangleright}^k {\underline n}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
This follows from Lemma~\ref{soundnesscompadequacyprop} and
  Lemma~\ref{refltransassumstep}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Let $R$ be relation on a type $X$. If
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{assump-1} $X$ has decidable equality;
  \item\label{assump-2} $R$ is single-valued;
  \item\label{assump-3} $\sum_{y : X} x R y$ is decidable for every $x : X$;
  \end{enumerate}
  then, the $k$-step reflexive transitive closure $R^k$ of $R$ is decidable for
  every natural number $k$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- therm-10: body_md -->
\label{semidecidablepcfprops}
  The propositions that arise from PCF terms $t$ of type $\iota$ are all
  semidecidable, as witnessed by the following logical equivalence:
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathsf{isdefined}}(\densem{t}) \longleftrightarrow \exists_{n : \mathsf{N}} \exists_{k :
      \mathsf{N}}\, t \mathbin{\triangleright}^k \underline n
  \]
  and the decidability of $t \mathbin{\triangleright}^k \underline n$.
<!-- end therm-10 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
A \emph{relation on $X$} is a term of type $X \to X \to \Omega$.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
Let $R$ be
  a relation on a type $X$. We wish to define the $k$-step reflexive transitive
  closure of $R$. As in Definition~\ref{def:refltransclos}, we want this to be
  proposition-valued again. Therefore, we proceed as follows. For any natural
  number $k$, define $x R_{k} y$ by induction on $k$:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $x R_{0}y \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv x = y$;
  \item $x R_{k+1}z \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \sum_{y : X} x R y \times y R_{k} z$.
  \end{enumerate}
  The \emph{$k$-step reflexive transitive closure $R^k$ of $R$} is now defined
  as the relation on $X$ given by ${x R^k y \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \squash{ x R_k y}}$.
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
Let $R$ be a relation on $X$. Recall the untruncated reflexive transitive
  closure $R_\ast$ from Definition~\ref{def:refltransclos}. We have a logical
  equivalence for every $x,y$ in $X$\textup{:}
  \[
    x R_\ast y \longleftrightarrow \sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} x R_{k} y.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Define $x R' y$ inductively by:
  \begin{alignat*}{2}
    &\mathsf{refl'} &&: \prod_{x : X} x R' x; \\
    &\mathsf{left} &&: \prod_{x y z : X} x R y \to y R' z \to x R' z.
  \end{alignat*}
  It is not hard to verify that $R'$ is reflexive, transitive and that it
  extends $R$. Using this, one shows that $x R' y$ and $x R_\ast y$ are
  logically equivalent for every $x,y : X$. Now one easily proves
  $\prod_{k : \mathsf{N}} (x R_k y \to x R' y)$ by induction on $k$. This yields
  $\pa*{\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} x R_k y} \to x R' y$. The converse is also easily
  established. Thus, $x R' y$ and $\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} x R_k y$ are logically
  equivalent, finishing the proof.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{refltransassumstep}
  Let $R$ be a relation on $X$. For every $x,y : X$, we have a logical
  equivalence:
  \[
    x R^\ast y \longleftrightarrow \squash*{\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} x R^k y}.
  \]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Let $x$ and $y$ be in $X$. By the previous lemma and functoriality of
  propositional truncation, we have
  \[
    x R^\ast y \equiv \squash{x R_\ast y} \longleftrightarrow \squash*{\sum_{k :
        \mathsf{N}} x R_k y}.
  \]
  But the latter is equivalent to
  $\squash*{\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}} \squash*{x R_k y}} \equiv \squash*{\sum_{k : \mathsf{N}}
    x R^k y}$ by \cite[Theorem 7.3.9]{HoTTbook}. This may also be proved
  directly, as done in the formalisation.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
A relation $R$ on $X$ is said to be \emph{single-valued} if for every
  $x,y,z : X$ with $x R y$ and $x R z$ we have $y = z$.
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
A relation $R$ on $X$ is said to be \emph{decidable} if the type $x R y$ is
  decidable for every $x$ and $y$ in $X$.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{decidablesquash}
  Let $X$ be a type. If $X$ is decidable, then so is $\squash{X}$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Suppose that $X$ is decidable. Then there are two cases to consider. Either we
  have $x : X$ or $\lnot X$. If we have $x : X$, then obviously we have
  $|x| : \squash{X}$.

  So suppose that $\lnot X$. We claim that $\lnot\squash{X}$. Assuming
  $\squash{X}$, we must find a term of type~$\mathsf{0}$. But $\mathsf{0}$ is a
  proposition, so we may actually assume that we have $x : X$. Using $\lnot X$,
  we then obtain~$\mathsf{0}$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- therm-11: body_md -->
\label{decidablekstep}
  Let $R$ be relation on a type $X$. If
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{cond-1} $X$ has decidable equality;
  \item\label{cond-2} $R$ is single-valued;
  \item\label{cond-3} $\sum_{y : X} x R y$ is decidable for every $x : X$;
  \end{enumerate}
  then, the $k$-step reflexive transitive closure $R^k$ of $R$ is decidable for
  every natural number $k$.
<!-- end therm-11 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Suppose $X$ and $R$ satisfy conditions \eqref{cond-1}--\eqref{cond-3}. By
  Lemma~\ref{decidablesquash}, it suffices to prove that the untruncated version
  of $R^k$, that is $R_k$, is decidable by induction on $k$.

  For the base case, let $x$ and $y$ be elements of $X$. We need to decide
  $x R_0 y$. By definition this means deciding $x = y$, which we can, since $X$
  is assumed to have decidable equality.

  Now suppose $x$ and $z$ are elements of $X$ and that $a R_k b$ is decidable
  for every $a,b : X$. We need to show that $xR_{k+1}z$ is decidable. By
  definition this means that we must prove
  \begin{equation*}\label{toprovedec}
    \sum_{y : X} x R y \times y R_k z \tag{$\ast$}
  \end{equation*}
  to be decidable. By~\eqref{cond-3}, we can decide $\sum_{y : X}x R y$. Obviously, if we
  have $\lnot\sum_{y : X}x R y$, then $\lnot\eqref{toprovedec}$. So assume that
  we have $y : X$ such that $x R y$. By induction hypothesis, $y R_k z$ is
  decidable. If we have $y R_k z$, then we get $\eqref{toprovedec}$. So suppose
  that $\lnot y R_k z$. We claim that $\lnot\eqref{toprovedec}$. For suppose
  $\eqref{toprovedec}$, then we obtain $y' : X$ with $x R y'$ and $y' R_k
  z$. But $R$ is single-valued, so $y = y'$ and hence, $y R_k z$, contradicting
  our assumption.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
Let $A$ and $I$ be types and let $B$ be a type family over $A$. Suppose we
  have $t : A \to I$ and $s : \pa*{\sum_{a : A} B(a)} \to I$. The \emph{indexed
    $\mathsf W$-type $\mathsf{W}_{s,t}$ specified by $s$~and~$t$} is the
  inductive type family over $I$ generated by the following constructor:
  \[
    \mathsf{indexedsup} : \prod_{a : A}\big(B(a) \to
    \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(s(a,b))\big) \to \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(t(a)).
  \]
  We have the following induction principle for indexed $\mathsf{W}$-types. If
  $E : \prod_{i : I}\pa*{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i) \to \mathcal U}$, then to prove
  $\prod_{i : I}\prod_{w : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)} E(i,w)$, it suffices to show
  that for any $a : A$ and $f : \prod_{b:B(a)}\mathsf{W}_{s,t}(s(a,b))$
  satisfying $E(s(a,b),f(b))$ for every $b : B(a)$ (the \emph{induction
    hypothesis}), we have a term of type $E(t(a),\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f))$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{termsasindexedWtype}
  In this example, we show that a fragment of the PCF terms can be encoded as an
  indexed $\mathsf{W}$-type. One could extend the encoding to capture all PCF
  terms, but we do not spell out the tedious details here, as a fragment
  suffices to get the idea across.

  The type family $\mathsf{T}$ is inductively defined as:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item $\mathsf{zero}$ is a term of type $\iota$;
  \item $\mathsf{succ}$ is a term of type $\iota \Rightarrow \iota$;
  \item for every PCF type $\sigma$ and $\tau$, we have a term
    $\mathsf{app}_{\sigma,\tau}$ of type
    $(\sigma \Rightarrow \tau) \Rightarrow \sigma \Rightarrow \tau$.
  \end{enumerate}
  We can encode $\mathsf{T}$ as an indexed $\mathsf{W}$-type. Let us write
  $\mathsf{2}$ for $\mathsf{1} + \mathsf{1}$ and $0_{\mathsf{2}}$ and $1_{\mathsf{2}}$
  for its elements. Take $I$ to be the type of PCF types and put
  $A \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{2} + (I \times I)$. Define $B : A \to \mathcal U$ by
  \[
    B(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(0_{\mathsf{2}})) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv B(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(1_{\mathsf{2}}))
    \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{0}\quad\text{and}\quad B(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\sigma,\tau))
    \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{2}.
  \]
  Finally, define $t$ by
  \[
    t(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(0_{\mathsf{2}})) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \iota;\quad
    t(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(1_{\mathsf{2}})) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \iota \Rightarrow \iota;\quad
    \text{and}\quad t(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\sigma,\tau)) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \tau;
  \]
  and $s$ by
  \[
    s(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\sigma,\tau),0_{\mathsf{2}}) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \sigma \Rightarrow
    \tau;\quad\text{and}\quad s(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\sigma,\tau),1_{\mathsf{2}})
    \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \sigma;
  \]
  on the other elements $s$ is defined as the unique function from $\mathsf{0}$.

  One can check that given a PCF type $\sigma : I$, there is a type equivalence
  $T(\sigma) \simeq W_{s,t}(\sigma)$.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{picompact}
  A type $X$ is called \emph{$\Pi$-compact} when every type family $Y$ over $X$
  satisfies: if $Y(x)$ is decidable for every $x : X$, then so is the dependent
  product $\prod_{x : X} Y(x)$.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{emptyunitpicompact}
  The empty type $\mathsf{0}$ is vacuously $\Pi$-compact. The unit type $\mathsf{1}$ is
  also easily seen to be $\Pi$-compact. There are also interesting examples of
  infinite types that are $\Pi$-compact, such as $\mathsf{N}_{\infty}$, the one-point
  compactification of the natural numbers
  \cite[\texttt{WeaklyCompactTypes}]{TypeTopology}.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- therm-12: body_md -->
\label{indexedWtypedeceq'}
  Let $A$ and $I$ be types and $B$ a type family over $A$. Suppose $t : A \to I$
  and $s : \pa*{\sum_{a : A}B(a)} \to I$. If $A$ has decidable equality, $B(a)$
  is $\Pi$-compact for every $a : A$ and $I$ is a set, then
  $\mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$ has decidable equality for every $i : I$.
<!-- end therm-12 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{decidableiff}
  Let $X$ and $Y$ be logically equivalent types. The type $X$ is decidable if
  and only if $Y$ is decidable.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Straightforward.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
A type $X$ is called a \emph{retract} of a type $Y$ if there are maps
  $s : X \to Y$ (the~\emph{section}) and $r : Y \to X$ (the \emph{retraction})
  such that $\prod_{x : X} r(s(x)) = x$.
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{retractdeceq}
  Let $X$ be a retract of $Y$. If $Y$ has decidable equality, then so does $X$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $r : Y \to X$ and $s : X \to Y$ be respectively the retraction and section
  establishing $X$ as a retract of $Y$. Let $a,b : X$. Since $Y$ has decidable
  equality, we can consider two cases: $r(a) = r(b)$ and $r(a) \neq r(b)$.
  In the first case, we find $a = s(r(a)) = s(r(b)) = b$. In the second case, we
  immediately see that $a \neq b$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{coproductpicompact}
  The $\Pi$-compact types are closed under binary coproducts.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
Let $X$ and $Y$ be $\Pi$-compact types. Suppose $F$ is a type family over
  $X + Y$ such that $F(z)$ is decidable for every $z : X + Y$. We must show that
  $\prod_{z : X + Y}F(z)$ is decidable.

  Define $F_X : X \to \mathcal U$ by $F_X(x) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv F(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(x))$ and
  $F_Y : Y \to\mathcal U$ as $F_Y(y) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv F(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(y))$. By our
  assumption on $F$, the types $F_X(x)$ and $F_Y(y)$ are decidable for every
  $x : X$ and $y : Y$. Hence, since $X$ and $Y$ are assumed to be $\Pi$-compact,
  the dependent products $\prod_{x : X}F_X(x)$ and $\prod_{y : Y}F_Y(y)$ are
  decidable.

  Finally, $\prod_{z : X + Y}F(z)$ is logically equivalent to
  $\prod_{x : X}F_X(x) \times \prod_{y : Y}F_Y(y)$. Since the product of two
  decidable types is again decidable, an application of Lemma~\ref{decidableiff}
  now finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- therm-13: body_md -->
The PCF terms have decidable equality.
<!-- end therm-13 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
As with Example~\ref{termsasindexedWtype}, we only spell out the details for
  the fragment $\mathsf{T}$. Recall that $\mathsf{T}$ may be encoded as a
  $\mathsf{W}$-type, indexed by the PCF types. Using
  Example~\ref{emptyunitpicompact} and Lemma~\ref{coproductpicompact}, we see
  that $B(a)$ is $\Pi$-compact for every $a : A$. Note that $A$ has decidable
  equality if $I$ does. So it remains to prove that $I$, the type of PCF types,
  has decidable equality.

  This will be another application of Theorem~\ref{indexedWtypedeceq'}. Define
  $A' \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{2}$ and define $B' : A' \to \mathcal U$ by
  $B'(\operatorname{\mathsf{inl}}(\star)) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{0}$ and $B'(\operatorname{\mathsf{inr}}(\star)) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
  \mathsf{2}$. Let $t'$ and $s'$ be the unique functions to $\mathsf{1}$ from $A'$ and
  $\sum_{x : A'}B'(x)$, respectively. One quickly verifies that the type of PCF
  types is a retract of $\mathsf{W}_{s',t'}(\star)$. Observe that $B'(x)$ is
  $\Pi$-compact for every $x : A'$ because of Example~\ref{emptyunitpicompact}
  and Lemma~\ref{coproductpicompact}.  Finally, $\mathsf{1}$ and $A' \equiv 2$
  clearly have decidable equality, so by Theorem~\ref{indexedWtypedeceq'} the
  type $\mathsf{W}_{s',t'}(\star)$ has decidable equality. Thus, by
  Lemma~\ref{retractdeceq}, so do the PCF types.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
Let $f : X \to Y$ be a map. The \emph{fiber of $f$ over a point $y : Y$} is
  \[
    \mathsf{fib}_f(y) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \sum_{x : X}(f(x) = y).
  \]
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- therm-14: body_md -->
\label{indexedWtypedeceq}
  Let $A$ and $I$ be types and $B$ a type family over $A$. Suppose $t : A \to I$
  and $s : \pa*{\sum_{a : A}B(a)} \to I$. If $B(a)$ is $\Pi$-compact for every
  $a : A$ and the fiber of $t$ over $i$ has decidable equality for every
  $i : I$, then $\mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$ also has decidable equality for every
  $i : I$.
<!-- end therm-14 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Suppose that $A$ has decidable equality and $I$ is a set. We are to show that
  the fiber of $t$ over $i$ has decidable equality for every $i : I$. Let
  $i : I$ be arbitrary. Suppose we have $(a,p)$ and $(a',p')$ in the fiber of
  $t$ over $i$. Since $A$ has decidable equality, we can decide whether $a$ and
  $a'$ are equal or not. If they are not, then certainly $(a,p) \neq
  (a',p')$. If they are, then we claim that the dependent pairs $(a,p)$ and
  $(a',p')$ are also equal. If $e : a = a'$ is the supposed equality, then it
  suffices to show that $\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\lambda x : A.t(x) = i}(e,p) = p'$,
  but both these terms are paths in $I$ and $I$ is a set, so they must be equal.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{rightpairinj}
  Let $X$ be a type and let $Y$ be a type family over it. If $X$ is a set, then
  the right pair function is injective, in the following sense: if
  $(x,y) = (x,y')$ as terms of $\sum_{a : X}Y(a)$, then $y = y'$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Suppose $X$ is a set, $x : X$ and $y,y' : Y(x)$ with $e : (x,y) =
  (x,y')$. From $e$, we obtain $e_1 : x = x$ and
  $e_2 : \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{Y}(e_1,y) = y'$. Since $X$ is a set, we must have
  that $e_1 = \mathsf{refl}_{x}$, so that from $e_2$ we obtain a term of type
  $y \equiv \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^Y(\mathsf{refl}_{x},y) = y'$, as desired.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- definition-29: body_md -->
For each $i : I$, define
  \[
    \mathsf{sub}_i : \mathsf{W}_{s,t} (i) \to \sum_{p:\mathsf{fib}_t(i)}
    \prod_{b : B(\operatorname{\mathsf{pr_1}}(p))}\mathsf{W}_{s,t}( s(\operatorname{\mathsf{pr_1}}(p),b))
  \]
  by induction:
  \[
    \mathsf{sub}_{t(a)}(\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f)) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    \pa*{\pa*{a,\mathsf{refl}_{t(a)}},f}.
  \]
  For notational convenience, we will omit the subscript of $\mathsf{sub}$.
<!-- end definition-29 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{eqtosubtreeeq}
  Let $a : A$ and $f,g : \prod_{b : B(a)} \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(s(a,b))$. If the
  fiber of $t$ over $i$ has decidable equality for every $i : I$, then
  $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f) = \mathsf{indexedsup}(a,g)$ implies $f = g$.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Suppose $\mathsf{indexesup}(a,f) = \mathsf{indexedsup}(a,g)$. Then
  \[
    \pa*{\pa*{a,\mathsf{refl}_{t(a)}},f} \equiv
    \mathsf{sub}(\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f)) =
    \mathsf{sub}(\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,g)) \equiv
    \pa*{\pa*{a,\mathsf{refl}_{t(a)}},g}.
  \]
  As \(\mathsf{fib}_t(i)\) is decidable, it is a set by
  Hedberg's~Theorem~\cite[Theorem~7.2.5]{HoTTbook}. Therefore \(f = g\) by
  Lemma~\ref{rightpairinj}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- definition-30: body_md -->
\label{getfib}
  For every $i : I$, define a function
  $\mathsf{getfib}_i : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i) \to \mathsf{fib}_t(i)$ inductively by
  \[
    \mathsf{getfib}_{t(a)}(\mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f)) \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv
    (a,\mathsf{refl}_{t(a)}).
  \]
  In future use, we omit the subscript of $\mathsf{getfib}$.
<!-- end definition-30 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{getfibtransport}
  Let $i,j : I$ with a path $p : i = j$ and $w : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$. We have
  the following equality:
  \[
    \mathsf{getfib}(\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}}(p,w)) =
    (\operatorname{\mathsf{pr_1}}(\mathsf{getfib}(w)),\operatorname{\mathsf{pr_2}}(\mathsf{getfib}(w)) \mathbin{\bullet} p).
  \]
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
By path induction on $p$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{indexedWtypedeceqtransport}
  Suppose that $B(a)$ is $\Pi$-compact for every $a :A $ and that the fiber of
  $t$ over each $i : I$ has decidable equality. For any $i : I$,
  $u : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$, $j : I$, path $p : i = j$ and
  $v : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(j)$, the type
  \[
    \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}}(p,u) = v
  \]
  is decidable.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Suppose $i : I$ and $u : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$. We proceed by induction on $u$
  and so we assume that $u \equiv \mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f)$. The induction
  hypothesis reads:
  \begin{equation*}\label{IH}
    \prod_{b : B(a)}\prod_{j' : I}\prod_{p' : s(a,b) = j'}\prod_{v' :
      \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(j')} (\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}}(p',f(b))=v')
    \text{ is decidable }. \tag{$\ast$}
  \end{equation*}
  Suppose we have $j : I$ with path $p : t(a) = j$ and $v : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(j)$.
  By induction, we may assume that $v \equiv \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')$. We are
  tasked to show that
  \begin{equation*}\label{indexedsupdec}
    \operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}}(p, \mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f)) =
    \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f') \tag{$\dagger$}
  \end{equation*}
  is decidable, where $p : t(a) = t(a')$.

  By assumption the fiber of $t$ over $t(a')$ has decidable equality. Hence, we
  can decide if $\pa*{a',\mathsf{refl}_{t(a')}}$ and $(a,p)$ are equal or
  not. Suppose first that the pairs are not equal. We claim that in this case
  $\lnot \eqref{indexedsupdec}$. For suppose we had $e : \eqref{indexedsupdec}$,
  then
  \[
    \mathsf{ap}_{\mathsf{getfib}}(e) :
    \mathsf{getfib}(\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\mathsf{W}_{s,t}}(p,
    \mathsf{indexedsup}(a,f))) = \mathsf{getfib}(\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')).
  \]
  By definition, the right hand side is $(a',\mathsf{refl}_{t(a')})$. By
  Lemma~\ref{getfibtransport}, the left hand side is equal to
  $(a, \mathsf{refl}_{t(a)} \mathbin{\bullet} p)$ which is in turn equal to $(a,p)$,
  contradicting our assumption that $\pa*{a',\mathsf{refl}_{t(a')}}$ and $(a,p)$
  were not equal.

  Now suppose that $\pa*{a',\mathsf{refl}_{t(a')}} = (a,p)$. From this, we
  obtain paths $e_1 : a' = a$ and
  $e_2~:~\operatorname{\mathsf{transport}}^{\lambda x : A.t(x) =
    t(a')}\pa*{e_1,\mathsf{refl}_{t(a')}} = p$. By path induction, we may assume
  $e_1 \equiv \mathsf{refl}_{a'}$, so that from $e_2$ we obtain a path
  \[
    \rho : \mathsf{refl}_{t(a')} = p.
  \]
  Using this path, we see that the left hand side of \eqref{indexedsupdec} is
  equal to $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f)$, so we are left to show that
  \[
    \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f) = \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')
  \]
  is decidable.

  By induction hypothesis \eqref{IH} and the fact that $a \equiv a'$, the type
  $ f(b) = f'(b) $ is decidable for every $b : B(a')$. Since $B(a')$ is
  $\Pi$-compact, this implies that $\prod_{b : B(a')}f(b) = f'(b)$ is decidable.

  Suppose first that $\prod_{b : B(a')}f(b) = f'(b)$. Function extensionality
  then yields $f = f'$, so that
  $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f) = \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')$.

  On the other hand, suppose $\lnot\prod_{b : B(a')}f(b) = f'(b)$. We claim that
  then, $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f)$ cannot be equal to
  $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')$. For suppose that
  $\mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f) = \mathsf{indexedsup}(a',f')$. Then
  Lemma~\ref{eqtosubtreeeq} yields $f = f'$, contradicting our assumption that
  $\lnot\prod_{b : B(a)}f(b) = f'(b)$, and finishing the proof.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Let $i : I$ and $u,v : \mathsf{W}_{s,t}(i)$. Taking $j \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv i$ and
  $p \vcentcolon\mspace{-1.2mu}\equiv \mathsf{refl}_i$ in Lemma~\ref{indexedWtypedeceqtransport}, we
  see that $u = v$ is decidable, as desired.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- therm-15: body_md -->
\label{interpretationtyped}
  The interpretation function $\densem{-}$ from PCF types to dcpos with $\bot$
  can be typed~as:
  \[
    \densem{-} : \textup{PCF types} \to \mathcal
    U_0\text{-}\pa*{\mathsf{DCPO}_\bot}_{\mathcal U_1,\mathcal U_1}.
  \]
<!-- end therm-15 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
If, in \eqref{universes-exponential}, we take $\mathcal W$ to be
  $\mathcal U_0$ and $\mathcal U,\mathcal U',\mathcal V,\mathcal V'$ all to be
  $\mathcal U_1$, then \eqref{universes-exponential} reads:
  \[
    (-)^{(-)} : \mathcal U_0\text{-}\pa*{\mathsf{DCPO}_\bot}_{\mathcal
      U_1,\mathcal U_1} \to \mathcal
    U_0\text{-}\pa*{\mathsf{DCPO}_\bot}_{\mathcal U_1,\mathcal U_1} \to \mathcal
    U_0\text{-}\pa*{\mathsf{DCPO}_\bot}_{\mathcal U_1,\mathcal U_1},
  \]
  as desired.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
